On the other hand, for any integer $t$ we have the exact sequence \[  egin{array}{ccccccccccccccccccc} 0 & ightarrow & [I_C]_{t-1} & ightarrow & [I_C]_t & ightarrow & [I_{\Gamma|H} ]_t & \longrightarrow & H^1(\mathcal I_C(t-1)) & ightarrow & \dots \ &&&&&&\hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \searrow & & 
earrow \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \ &&&&&&& [K]_t \ &&&&&&\hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ } 
earrow & & \searrow \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \ &&&&&&\hbox{\ } 0 & & 0 \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ } \ \end{array} \] (where $K$ is just the cokernel). Then after adding and subtracting some binomial coefficients and setting $ ar R = R/L$, we obtain \[  egin{array}{rcl} \Delta h_{R/I_C} (t) & = & h_{ ar R/I_{\Gamma|H}}(t) + \dim [K]_t \ & \geq & h_{ ar R/I_{\Gamma | H}} (t). \end{array} \] So since $\ell \gg 0$ we obtain \[  egin{array}{rcl} g_C & = & 1 + d\ell - h_{R/I_C}(\ell) \ & = & d\ell - \sum_{t=1}^\ell \Delta h_{R/I_C}(t) \ & \leq & d\ell - \sum_{t=1}^\ell h_{ ar R/I_{\Gamma|H}} (t) \ & = & \sum_{t=1}^\ell \left [ d - h_{ ar R/I_{\Gamma | H}} (t) ight ]. \end{array} \] Now replace $C$ by $D$, and replace $\Gamma$ by the hyperplane section of $D$, which is a set of $d$ collinear points, say $A$. We have, similarly, \[ g_D = \sum_{t=1}^\ell \left [ d - h_{ ar R/I_A}(t) ight ] =  inom{d-1}{2} . \] It is clear that for any $t \geq 1$ we have \[ h_{ ar R/I_{\Gamma|H}} (t) \geq h_{ ar R/I_A}(t) \] with strict inequality for $t=1$, so we obtain $g_C < g_D$. This completes the proof of Claim 1. Now, by \cite{GLP} Remark (1) (p. 497), we have $H^1(\mathcal I_C(d)) = H^2(\mathcal I_C(d)) = 0$, and we also have $H^1(\mathcal I_D(d)) = H^2(\mathcal I_D(d)) = 0$. Consider the exact sequence \[ 0 ightarrow [I_C]_d ightarrow H^0(\mathcal O_{\PP^3}(d)) ightarrow H^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) ightarrow H^1(\mathcal I_C(d)) ightarrow 0. \] \medskip 
oindent \underline{Claim 2}: {\em Let $D$ be a plane curve of degree $d$. Then $h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) > h^0(\mathcal O_D(d))$.} \medskip Indeed, \[  egin{array}{rcl} d^2 - g_C + 1 & = & h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) - h^1(\mathcal O_C(d)) \ & = & h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) - h^2(\mathcal I_C(d)) \ & = & h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) \end{array} \] and similarly for $D$, so thanks to Claim 1 we have \[ h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) > h^0(\mathcal O_D(d)) \] and we have Claim 2. Then \[  egin{array}{rcll} \dim [I_C]_d & = & \displaystyle  inom{d+3}{3} - h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) & \hbox{(since } h^1(\mathcal I_C(d)) = 0 ) \ \ & < & \displaystyle  inom{d+3}{3} - h^0(\mathcal O_D(d)) \end{array} \] thanks to Claim 2. To check that $S_P$ is an unexpected surface it is enough to note that \[  egin{array}{rcl} \displaystyle \dim [I_C]_d -  inom{d-1+3}{3} & < & \displaystyle  inom{d+3}{3} - h^0(\mathcal O_D(d)) -  inom{d-1+3}{3} \ \ & = & \displaystyle  inom{d+2}{2} - [d^2 - g_D + 1] \ \ & = & 1 \end{array} \] using the value of $g_D$ mentioned above.
nodes.statement_short: Bezout gives uniqueness; then compare the arithmetic genus and $h^0$ of $C$ with a plane curve of the same degree to force a one-dimensional excess.

nodes.name: uniqueness via Bezout
nodes.statement: We first check uniqueness. Let $F$ be a form defining a surface containing $C$, of degree $d$ with multiplicity $d$ at $P$. Let $\lambda$ be a line through $P$ and any point $Q$, of $C$. Then by B\'ezout, $F$ must vanish on all of $\lambda$. Thus the surface defined by $F$ is precisely $S_P$.
nodes.statement_short: Bezout forces any such $F$ to vanish on every line from $P$ to $C$, so the surface is $S_P$.

nodes.name: set up the genus comparison
nodes.statement: We now check unexpectedness. Let $D$ be a smooth plane curve of degree $d$. \medskip \noindent \underline{Claim 1}: {\em The arithmetic genus, $g_C$, of $C$ is strictly less than that of $D$, which is $g_D = \binom{d-1}{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce a smooth plane curve $D$ of degree $d$ and state Claim 1 comparing arithmetic genera.

nodes.name: prove Claim 1
nodes.statement: This argument is classical. Much of it is given in \cite{harris} (when C is irreducible) and in \cite{migbook} Proposition 1.4.2, so no claim is made to originality; we include it here just for the reader's convenience. Let $\Gamma$ be a general hyperplane section of $C$ by a hyperplane $H$ defined by a general linear form $L$. Let $I_{\Gamma | H}$ be the saturated ideal of $\Gamma$ in $H$. Let $\ell \gg 0$. Then \[ \begin{array}{rcl} d\ell - g_C + 1 & = & h^0(\mathcal O_C(\ell)) \\ & = & h_{R/I_C}(\ell) \end{array} \] where $h_{R/I_C}(t)$ is the Hilbert function of $C$. On the other hand, for any integer $t$ we have the exact sequence \[ \begin{array}{ccccccccccccccccccc} 0 & \rightarrow & [I_C]_{t-1} & \rightarrow & [I_C]_t & \rightarrow & [I_{\Gamma|H} ]_t & \longrightarrow & H^1(\mathcal I_C(t-1)) & \rightarrow & \dots \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \searrow & & \nearrow \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ &&&&&&& [K]_t \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \nearrow & & \searrow \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ } 0 & & 0 \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ \end{array} \] (where $K$ is just the cokernel). Then after adding and subtracting some binomial coefficients and setting $\bar R = R/L$, we obtain \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \Delta h_{R/I_C} (t) & = & h_{\bar R/I_{\Gamma|H}}(t) + \dim [K]_t \\ & \geq & h_{\bar R/I_{\Gamma | H}} (t). \end{array} \] So since $\ell \gg 0$ we obtain \[ \begin{array}{rcl} g_C & = & 1 + d\ell - h_{R/I_C}(\ell) \\ & = & d\ell - \sum_{t=1}^\ell \Delta h_{R/I_C}(t) \\ & \leq & d\ell - \sum_{t=1}^\ell h_{\bar R/I_{\Gamma|H}} (t) \\ & = & \sum_{t=1}^\ell \left [ d - h_{\bar R/I_{\Gamma | H}} (t) \right ]. \end{array} \] Now replace $C$ by $D$, and replace $\Gamma$ by the hyperplane section of $D$, which is a set of $d$ collinear points, say $A$. We have, similarly, \[ g_D = \sum_{t=1}^\ell \left [ d - h_{\bar R/I_A}(t) \right ] = \binom{d-1}{2} . \] It is clear that for any $t \geq 1$ we have \[ h_{\bar R/I_{\Gamma|H}} (t) \geq h_{\bar R/I_A}(t) \] with strict inequality for $t=1$, so we obtain $g_C < g_D$. This completes the proof of Claim 1.
nodes.statement_short: Compare Hilbert functions of general hyperplane sections to get $g_C<g_D$.

nodes.name: cohomology vanishing and the restriction sequence
nodes.statement: Now, by \cite{GLP} Remark (1) (p. 497), we have $H^1(\mathcal I_C(d)) = H^2(\mathcal I_C(d)) = 0$, and we also have $H^1(\mathcal I_D(d)) = H^2(\mathcal I_D(d)) = 0$. Consider the exact sequence \[ 0 \rightarrow [I_C]_d \rightarrow H^0(\mathcal O_{\PP^3}(d)) \rightarrow H^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) \rightarrow H^1(\mathcal I_C(d)) \rightarrow 0.
nodes.statement_short: Invoke Gruson-Lazarsfeld-Peskine vanishing and write the degree-$d$ restriction sequence.

nodes.name: prove Claim 2
nodes.statement: Indeed, \[ \begin{array}{rcl} d^2 - g_C + 1 & = & h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) - h^1(\mathcal O_C(d)) \\ & = & h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) - h^2(\mathcal I_C(d)) \\ & = & h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) \end{array} \] and similarly for $D$, so thanks to Claim 1 we have \[ h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) > h^0(\mathcal O_D(d)) \] and we have Claim 2.
nodes.statement_short: Riemann-Roch plus Claim 1 give $h^0(\mathcal O_C(d))>h^0(\mathcal O_D(d))$.

nodes.name: conclude unexpectedness
nodes.statement: Then \[ \begin{array}{rcll} \dim [I_C]_d & = & \displaystyle \binom{d+3}{3} - h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) & \hbox{(since } h^1(\mathcal I_C(d)) = 0 ) \\ \\ & < & \displaystyle \binom{d+3}{3} - h^0(\mathcal O_D(d)) \end{array} \] thanks to Claim 2. To check that $S_P$ is an unexpected surface it is enough to note that \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \displaystyle \dim [I_C]_d - \binom{d-1+3}{3} & < & \displaystyle \binom{d+3}{3} - h^0(\mathcal O_D(d)) - \binom{d-1+3}{3} \\ \\ & = & \displaystyle \binom{d+2}{2} - [d^2 - g_D + 1] \\ \\ & = & 1 \end{array} \] using the value of $g_D$ mentioned above.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $\dim[I_C]_d-\binom{d+2}{3}<1$, so the cone is unexpected.

nodes.name: Proof that a general hyperplane section stays non-degenerate
nodes.statement: We have the exact sequence \[ 0 \rightarrow [I_V]_0 \rightarrow [I_V]_1 \rightarrow [I_{W|H}]_1 \rightarrow H^1(\mathcal I_V (0)) \rightarrow \dots \] We want to show that the third vector space in this exact sequence is zero. But $[I_V]_1 = 0$ since $V$ is non-degenerate. On the other hand, we claim that $H^1(\mathcal I_V(0)) = 0$. This will complete the proof. But we also have the exact sequence \[ 0 \rightarrow [I_V]_0 \rightarrow [R]_0 \rightarrow H^0(\mathcal O_V(0)) \rightarrow H^1(\mathcal I_V(0)) \rightarrow 0. \] The first term is clearly zero. The second has dimension 1. The third has dimension 1 since $V$ is connected (being of codimension 2 and equidimensional) and reduced (by hypothesis). Thus the claim follows.
nodes.statement_short: Chase two short exact sequences and use connectedness of $V$ to force $H^1(\mathcal I_V(0))=0$.

nodes.name: restriction sequence in degree 1
nodes.statement: We have the exact sequence \[ 0 \rightarrow [I_V]_0 \rightarrow [I_V]_1 \rightarrow [I_{W|H}]_1 \rightarrow H^1(\mathcal I_V (0)) \rightarrow \dots
nodes.statement_short: Write the degree-1 restriction sequence for $V$ and $W=V\cap H$.

nodes.name: reduce to a cohomology vanishing
nodes.statement: We want to show that the third vector space in this exact sequence is zero. But $[I_V]_1 = 0$ since $V$ is non-degenerate. On the other hand, we claim that $H^1(\mathcal I_V(0)) = 0$. This will complete the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to showing $[I_{W|H}]_1=0$, hence to $H^1(\mathcal I_V(0))=0$.

nodes.name: compute $H^1(\mathcal I_V(0))$
nodes.statement: But we also have the exact sequence \[ 0 \rightarrow [I_V]_0 \rightarrow [R]_0 \rightarrow H^0(\mathcal O_V(0)) \rightarrow H^1(\mathcal I_V(0)) \rightarrow 0. \] The first term is clearly zero. The second has dimension 1. The third has dimension 1 since $V$ is connected (being of codimension 2 and equidimensional) and reduced (by hypothesis). Thus the claim follows.
nodes.statement_short: Connectedness and reducedness of $V$ make both middle terms one-dimensional, killing $H^1$.

nodes.name: Proof of the codimension-two cone proposition
nodes.statement: The proof is by induction on $n$. The initial case is Proposition \ref{cone in P3}, so we can assume $n \geq 4$. Let $H$ be a general hyperplane through $P$ and let $W = V \cap H$. Since $P$ is general, we can assume that $H$ is general as well. By Lemma \ref{nondeg}, $W$ is non-degenerate in $H = \PP^{n-1}$, and it is also reduced and equidimensional. Let $T_P$ be the cone in $H$ over $W$ with vertex $P$. Thus by induction, $T_P$ is the unique hypersurface of degree $d$ containing $W$ with multiplicity $d$ at $P$, and it is unexpected. Consider the exact sequence \[ \begin{array}{ccccccccccccccccccc} 0 & \rightarrow & [I_V]_{d-1} & \rightarrow & [I_V]_d & \rightarrow & [I_{W|H} ]_d & \longrightarrow & H^1(\mathcal I_V(d-1)) & \rightarrow & \dots \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \searrow & & \nearrow \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ &&&&&&& [K]_d \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \nearrow & & \searrow \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ } 0 & & 0 \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ \end{array} \] We have \[ \dim [I_V]_d = \dim [I_V]_{d-1} + \dim [I_{W|H}]_d - \dim [K]_d. \] We claim that \[ \dim [I_V]_d - \binom{d-1+n}{n} \leq 0 \] so that $S_P$ is unexpected. We have \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_d - \binom{d-1+n}{n} & = & \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_{d-1} + \left ( \dim [I_{W|H}]_d - \binom{d-1+(n-1)}{n-1} \right ) \\ \\ && \displaystyle + \binom{d-1+(n-1)}{n-1} - \dim [K]_d - \binom{d-1+n}{n} \\ \\ & \leq & \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_{d-1} + \binom{d+n-2}{n-1} - \dim [K]_d - \binom{d+n-1}{n} \\ \\ & = & \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_{d-1} - \binom{d+n-2}{n} - \dim [K]_d . \end{array} \] But Remark \ref{low deg rmk} gives \[ \dim [I_V]_{d-1} \leq \binom{d+n-2}{n}, \] which completes the claim. Uniqueness follows in the same way as it did for Proposition~\ref{cone in P3}.
nodes.statement_short: By induction on $n$, slicing with a general hyperplane through $P$ and applying the codimension-two bound of the earlier remark.

nodes.name: base case
nodes.statement: The proof is by induction on $n$. The initial case is Proposition \ref{cone in P3}, so we can assume $n \geq 4$.
nodes.statement_short: Set up induction on $n$ with the $\PP^3$ proposition as base case.

nodes.name: inductive hypothesis on the hyperplane section
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a general hyperplane through $P$ and let $W = V \cap H$. Since $P$ is general, we can assume that $H$ is general as well. By Lemma \ref{nondeg}, $W$ is non-degenerate in $H = \PP^{n-1}$, and it is also reduced and equidimensional. Let $T_P$ be the cone in $H$ over $W$ with vertex $P$. Thus by induction, $T_P$ is the unique hypersurface of degree $d$ containing $W$ with multiplicity $d$ at $P$, and it is unexpected.
nodes.statement_short: Slice by a general hyperplane through $P$ and apply the inductive hypothesis to $W$.

nodes.name: restriction sequence in degree $d$
nodes.statement: Consider the exact sequence \[ \begin{array}{ccccccccccccccccccc} 0 & \rightarrow & [I_V]_{d-1} & \rightarrow & [I_V]_d & \rightarrow & [I_{W|H} ]_d & \longrightarrow & H^1(\mathcal I_V(d-1)) & \rightarrow & \dots \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \searrow & & \nearrow \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ &&&&&&& [K]_d \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \nearrow & & \searrow \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ } 0 & & 0 \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ \end{array} \] We have \[ \dim [I_V]_d = \dim [I_V]_{d-1} + \dim [I_{W|H}]_d - \dim [K]_d.
nodes.statement_short: Write the restriction sequence and read off the dimension identity.

nodes.name: estimate the excess
nodes.statement: We claim that \[ \dim [I_V]_d - \binom{d-1+n}{n} \leq 0 \] so that $S_P$ is unexpected. We have \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_d - \binom{d-1+n}{n} & = & \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_{d-1} + \left ( \dim [I_{W|H}]_d - \binom{d-1+(n-1)}{n-1} \right ) \\ \\ && \displaystyle + \binom{d-1+(n-1)}{n-1} - \dim [K]_d - \binom{d-1+n}{n} \\ \\ & \leq & \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_{d-1} + \binom{d+n-2}{n-1} - \dim [K]_d - \binom{d+n-1}{n} \\ \\ & = & \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_{d-1} - \binom{d+n-2}{n} - \dim [K]_d .
nodes.statement_short: Reduce the claim to a binomial estimate in terms of $\dim[I_V]_{d-1}$.

nodes.name: apply the low-degree remark and conclude
nodes.statement: But Remark \ref{low deg rmk} gives \[ \dim [I_V]_{d-1} \leq \binom{d+n-2}{n}, \] which completes the claim. Uniqueness follows in the same way as it did for Proposition~\ref{cone in P3}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the earlier remark's bound and repeat the Bezout uniqueness argument.

nodes.name: Proof for points spanning the same degree-$d$ ideal piece
nodes.statement: It is immediate from the hypothesis that $[I_C]_d = [I_Z]_d$.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the hypothesis $[I_C]_d=[I_Z]_d$.

nodes.name: Proof of the higher-degree cone corollary
nodes.statement: Let $Y = C \cup kP$. We want to show that \begin{equation} \max \left\{ 0 , \dim[I_C]_k - \binom{k+2}{3} \right\} < \dim [I_Y]_k. \end{equation} Modifying the calculation above, we know that \[ \dim [I_C]_k = \binom{k+3}{3} - [dk - g_C + 1] \] so \[ \dim [I_C]_k - \binom{k+2}{3} = \binom{k+2}{2} - dk + g_C -1. \] On the other hand, we have a unique surface $S_P$ of degree $d$ with a singularity of multiplicity $d$ at the general point $P$, so by multiplying $S_P$ by an element of $[I_P^{k-d}]_{k-d}$ we always obtain a surface of degree $k$ with multiplicity $k$ at $P$. Thus \[ \dim [I_Y]_k \geq \binom{k-d+2}{2}, \] in particular $\dim [I_Y]_k > 0$. Thus combining, it is enough to show \[ \binom{k+2}{2} - dk + g_C -1 < \binom{k-d+2}{2}. \] A calculation shows that this is equivalent to \[ g_C < \frac{(d-1)(d-2)}{2}, \] which we showed in Claim 1 of Proposition \ref{cone in P3}.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply the degree-$d$ cone by forms of degree $k-d$ to bound $\dim[I_Y]_k$ from below, then reduce to the genus bound of Claim 1.

nodes.name: state the inequality to be shown
nodes.statement: Let $Y = C \cup kP$. We want to show that \begin{equation} \max \left\{ 0 , \dim[I_C]_k - \binom{k+2}{3} \right\} < \dim [I_Y]_k. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Set $Y=C\cup kP$ and record the inequality that expresses unexpectedness.

nodes.name: compute the expected dimension
nodes.statement: Modifying the calculation above, we know that \[ \dim [I_C]_k = \binom{k+3}{3} - [dk - g_C + 1] \] so \[ \dim [I_C]_k - \binom{k+2}{3} = \binom{k+2}{2} - dk + g_C -1.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\dim[I_C]_k-\binom{k+2}{3}$ in terms of $g_C$.

nodes.name: lower bound for $\dim [I_Y]_k$
nodes.statement: On the other hand, we have a unique surface $S_P$ of degree $d$ with a singularity of multiplicity $d$ at the general point $P$, so by multiplying $S_P$ by an element of $[I_P^{k-d}]_{k-d}$ we always obtain a surface of degree $k$ with multiplicity $k$ at $P$. Thus \[ \dim [I_Y]_k \geq \binom{k-d+2}{2}, \] in particular $\dim [I_Y]_k > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Multiplying $S_P$ by degree $k-d$ forms vanishing to order $k-d$ at $P$ gives $\dim[I_Y]_k\ge\binom{k-d+2}{2}$.

nodes.name: reduce to the genus bound
nodes.statement: Thus combining, it is enough to show \[ \binom{k+2}{2} - dk + g_C -1 < \binom{k-d+2}{2}. \] A calculation shows that this is equivalent to \[ g_C < \frac{(d-1)(d-2)}{2}, \] which we showed in Claim 1 of Proposition \ref{cone in P3}.

nodes.name: Proof of the corollary obtained by adding a hypersurface
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be the form defining $S$. Then \[ [I_Z]_{d+e} = [I_Y]_{d+e} = F \cdot [I_V]_d \] so \[ \dim [I_Z]_{d+e} - \binom{d+n-1}{n} = \dim [I_V]_d - \binom{d+n-1}{n} < 1 \] as we saw in the proof of Proposition \ref{Pn}. Thus $S_P \cup S$ is an unexpected hypersurface of degree $d+e$ with a singular point of multiplicity $d$ at $P$.
nodes.statement_short: Factor $[I_Y]_{d+e}=F\cdot[I_V]_d$ and reuse the dimension count from the codimension-two proposition.

nodes.name: factor the ideal piece
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be the form defining $S$. Then \[ [I_Z]_{d+e} = [I_Y]_{d+e} = F \cdot [I_V]_d \] so \[ \dim [I_Z]_{d+e} - \binom{d+n-1}{n} = \dim [I_V]_d - \binom{d+n-1}{n} < 1 \] as we saw in the proof of Proposition \ref{Pn}.
nodes.statement_short: Write $[I_Z]_{d+e}=F\cdot[I_V]_d$ and transfer the earlier dimension estimate.

nodes.name: conclude
nodes.statement: Thus $S_P \cup S$ is an unexpected hypersurface of degree $d+e$ with a singular point of multiplicity $d$ at $P$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude that $S_P\cup S$ is the required unexpected hypersurface.

nodes.name: Proof of the existence classification
nodes.statement: For (i), we first note that there is an unexpected curve of degree $m+1$ and multiplicity $m$ at a general point for each $m \geq 3$. Indeed, \begin{itemize} \item $m \leq 2$. It was shown by Akesseh \cite{A} that this occurs only in characteristic 2. (See also \cite{FGST} for a different proof that shows that it does not occur in characteristic zero.) \item $m=3$. This comes from the dual of the $B_3$ arrangement \cite{DIV}. \item $m=4$. Consider the line arrangement defined by the linear factors of $$xyz(x^3-y^3)(x^3-z^3)(y^3-z^3).$$ This is a supersolvable arrangement (see definition in \S\ref{root system section}), so Theorem 3.7 of \cite{DMO} applies. In particular, the dual points give a reduced set of 12 points which admit an unexpected curve with $d=5$ and $m=4$. \item $m=5$. This follows from \cite{CHMN} Proposition 6.15, taking $k=2$. \item $m \geq 6$. This comes from the points dual to the Fermat arrangement, by \cite{CHMN} Proposition 6.15, taking $t \geq 5$. \end{itemize} \noindent It is clear that a set of points $Z$ in $\PP^2$ cannot admit an unexpected curve whose degree and multiplicity at a general point $P$ are equal (unlike what we have seen in $\PP^3$). Indeed, in this situation the line joining $P$ to any point of $Z$ must be a component of such an unexpected curve, so the unexpected curve is a cone with vertex $P$ over the points of $Z$. Let $d = \deg Z$ be the degree of this curve. Then $Z$ imposes independent conditions on curves of degree $d$, so $\dim [I_Z]_d = \binom{d+2}{2} - d$. Then \[ \dim [I_Z]_d - \binom{(d-1)+2}{2} = \binom{d+2}{2} - d - \binom{d+1}{2} = (d+1)-d = 1 \] so in fact the cone is not unexpected. Thus $m < d$. With this preparation, we use the same argument as was used to prove Corollary \ref{add S}. Let $Z_0$ be a set of points admitting an unexpected curve of degree $m+1$ and multiplicity $m$ at a general point $P$ and let $A$ be a plane curve of degree $d-m-1$ not passing through any point of $Z_0$. Since $P$ is general, it does not lie on $A$. Then choosing sufficiently many points on $A$ gives a unique unexpected curve of degree $d$ and multiplicity $m$ at $P$. (A similar construction also was used in \cite[Proposition 6.7]{DIV}, but see \cite[Example 7.4]{CHMN}.) Part (ii) follows from Proposition \ref{Pn} and Corollary \ref{add S}.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on $m$ supplies plane examples, a Bezout argument rules out $d=m$ in $\PP^2$, and part (ii) follows from the cone construction.

nodes.name: case $m \leq 2$
nodes.statement: $m \leq 2$. It was shown by Akesseh \cite{A} that this occurs only in characteristic 2. (See also \cite{FGST} for a different proof that shows that it does not occur in characteristic zero.)
nodes.statement_short: In characteristic zero no unexpected curve occurs for $m\le2$.

nodes.name: case $m=3$
nodes.statement: $m=3$. This comes from the dual of the $B_3$ arrangement
nodes.statement_short: The $B_3$ arrangement supplies the $m=3$ example.

nodes.name: case $m=4$
nodes.statement: $m=4$. Consider the line arrangement defined by the linear factors of $$xyz(x^3-y^3)(x^3-z^3)(y^3-z^3).$$ This is a supersolvable arrangement (see definition in \S\ref{root system section}), so Theorem 3.7 of \cite{DMO} applies. In particular, the dual points give a reduced set of 12 points which admit an unexpected curve with $d=5$ and $m=4$.

nodes.name: case $m=5$
nodes.statement: $m=5$. This follows from \cite{CHMN} Proposition 6.15, taking $k=2$.
nodes.statement_short: Cite CHMN Proposition 6.15 with $k=2$.

nodes.name: rule out $d=m$ in the plane
nodes.statement: It is clear that a set of points $Z$ in $\PP^2$ cannot admit an unexpected curve whose degree and multiplicity at a general point $P$ are equal (unlike what we have seen in $\PP^3$). Indeed, in this situation the line joining $P$ to any point of $Z$ must be a component of such an unexpected curve, so the unexpected curve is a cone with vertex $P$ over the points of $Z$. Let $d = \deg Z$ be the degree of this curve. Then $Z$ imposes independent conditions on curves of degree $d$, so $\dim [I_Z]_d = \binom{d+2}{2} - d$. Then \[ \dim [I_Z]_d - \binom{(d-1)+2}{2} = \binom{d+2}{2} - d - \binom{d+1}{2} = (d+1)-d = 1 \] so in fact the cone is not unexpected. Thus $m < d$.
nodes.statement_short: If $d=m$ the curve would be a cone over $Z$, whose dimension count is exactly the expected one.

nodes.name: raise the degree by adding a plane curve
nodes.statement: With this preparation, we use the same argument as was used to prove Corollary \ref{add S}. Let $Z_0$ be a set of points admitting an unexpected curve of degree $m+1$ and multiplicity $m$ at a general point $P$ and let $A$ be a plane curve of degree $d-m-1$ not passing through any point of $Z_0$. Since $P$ is general, it does not lie on $A$. Then choosing sufficiently many points on $A$ gives a unique unexpected curve of degree $d$ and multiplicity $m$ at $P$. (A similar construction also was used in \cite[Proposition 6.7]{DIV}, but see \cite[Example 7.4]{CHMN}.)
nodes.statement_short: Add points on an auxiliary curve of degree $d-m-1$ to move from degree $m+1$ to degree $d$.

nodes.name: Proof of the SLP equivalence
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a general linear form. Consider the exact sequence \begin{equation} \dots \rightarrow [R/(L_1^d, \dots, L_{r}^d)]_{m-1} \stackrel{\times L^{d-m+1}}{\longrightarrow} [R/(L_1^{d},\dots,L_{r}^{d})]_{d} \rightarrow [R/(L_1^{d},\dots,L_{r}^{d},L^{d-m+1})]_{d} \rightarrow 0. \end{equation} Let $P$ be the general point of $\PP^n$ dual to $L$. By Macaulay duality \cite{EI} and exactness, \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \dim [I_Z \cap I_P^{m}]_{d} & = & \dim [R/(L_1^{d} , \dots, L_r^{d},L^{d-m+1})]_{d} \\ \\ & \geq & \dim [R/(L_1^d,\dots, L_r^d)]_d - \dim [R/(L_1^d,\dots,L_r^d)]_{m-1} \\ \\ & = & \displaystyle \dim [I_Z]_d - \binom{n+m-1}{n}. \end{array} \] Since (a) holds if and only if $\dim [I_Z \cap I_P^{m}]_{d}>\max(0, \dim [I_Z]_d - \binom{n+m-1}{n})$ if and only if $\dim [R/(L_1^{d} , \dots, L_r^{d},L^{d-m+1})]_{d}>\max(0, \dim [R/(L_1^d,\dots, L_r^d)]_d - \dim [R/(L_1^d,\dots,L_r^d)]_{m-1})$ if and only if (b) holds, the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Macaulay duality turns the multiplication-by-$L^{d-m+1}$ sequence into the dimension comparison defining unexpectedness.

nodes.name: the multiplication exact sequence
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a general linear form. Consider the exact sequence \begin{equation} \dots \rightarrow [R/(L_1^d, \dots, L_{r}^d)]_{m-1} \stackrel{\times L^{d-m+1}}{\longrightarrow} [R/(L_1^{d},\dots,L_{r}^{d})]_{d} \rightarrow [R/(L_1^{d},\dots,L_{r}^{d},L^{d-m+1})]_{d} \rightarrow 0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Right-exact multiplication sequence.

nodes.name: apply Macaulay duality
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be the general point of $\PP^n$ dual to $L$. By Macaulay duality \cite{EI} and exactness, \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \dim [I_Z \cap I_P^{m}]_{d} & = & \dim [R/(L_1^{d} , \dots, L_r^{d},L^{d-m+1})]_{d} \\ \\ & \geq & \dim [R/(L_1^d,\dots, L_r^d)]_d - \dim [R/(L_1^d,\dots,L_r^d)]_{m-1} \\ \\ & = & \displaystyle \dim [I_Z]_d - \binom{n+m-1}{n}.
nodes.statement_short: Macaulay duality identifies $\dim[I_Z\cap I_P^m]_d$ with the cokernel dimension.

nodes.name: chain the equivalences
nodes.statement: Since (a) holds if and only if $\dim [I_Z \cap I_P^{m}]_{d}>\max(0, \dim [I_Z]_d - \binom{n+m-1}{n})$ if and only if $\dim [R/(L_1^{d} , \dots, L_r^{d},L^{d-m+1})]_{d}>\max(0, \dim [R/(L_1^d,\dots, L_r^d)]_d - \dim [R/(L_1^d,\dots,L_r^d)]_{m-1})$ if and only if (b) holds, the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Chain the two strict inequalities to get (a) iff (b).

nodes.statement: The statement about linear general position is immediate since $C$ is reduced, irreducible and non-degenerate. nodes.name: Proof of WLP failure in $\PP^n$
nodes.statement: We recall that we can always find an irreducible, non-degenerate subvariety $V$ of codimension 2 and degree $k$ in $\PP^n$. In fact, if $k$ is even we take $V$ as an intersection of a general form of degree $\frac{k}{2}$ and a general quadric. If $k$ is odd we take $V$ as a general arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay subscheme with a minimal free resolution of the form \[ 0 \rightarrow R(- {\textstyle \frac{k+3}{2} })^2 \rightarrow R(- {\textstyle \frac{k+1}{2} })^2 \oplus R(-2) \rightarrow R \rightarrow R/I_V \rightarrow 0 \] (obtained, for example, by linking from a linear space of codimension 2 using the complete intersection of a quadric and a form of degree $\frac{k+1}{2}$). Using this sequence, or the Koszul resolution if $k$ is even, we obtain \[ \dim [R/I_V]_k = f (n, k). \] Since $V$ is irreducible, it makes sense to speak of a general set of points on $V$. Let $Z$ be a general set of $N$ points on $V$. From the generality of $Z$ we have \[ \dim [R/I_Z]_k = \min \{ \dim [R/I_V]_k , |Z| \}, \] hence $\dim [I_V]_k = \dim [I_Z]_k$. By Proposition 2.4 we then have that the cone over $V$ with vertex at a general point $P$ is an unexpected hypersurface of degree $k$ and multiplicity $k$ at $P$. Then the argument in the proof of Corollary 2.16 can be extended to our situation to show that the multiplication from degree $k-1$ to degree $k$ by a general linear form has an unexpectedly large cokernel, i.e. maximal rank does not hold. Since $Z$ is general on $V$ and $V$ is irreducible and non-degenerate, $Z$ is a set of points in linear general position, and this implies the condition on the linear forms not to have a common zero.
nodes.statement_short: Construct a codimension-two $V$ of degree $k$ (even/odd cases separately), take general points on it, and apply the cone proposition.

nodes.name: Proof of the properties of $F^*$ and $G^\circ$
nodes.statement: (a) Since $F=BF^*/H=B(F^*)^\circ a_0^t/H$, where $t=\deg(H)-\deg(B)$, we see that $F$ and $(F^*)^\circ$ differ by $Ba_0^t/H$, which is a unit in $S$. (b) Note that $F$ and $(F^*)^\circ$ differ by a unit factor in $S$, so one is irreducible if and only if the other is. Also, $F^*$ by construction has no factors of bi-degree $(f,0)$ with $f>0$, so if $F^*$ fails to be irreducible, it factors as $F^*=AB$ where $A$ and $B$ have bi-degree $(a,d_A)$ and $(b,d_B)$ with $d_A,d_B>0$ and $d_A+d_B=d$. But then $(F^*)^\circ=A^\circ B^\circ$ is a product of factors of positive degree and hence not irreducible. (c) If $G^\circ$ is not irreducible, then $G^\circ=AB$ where both $A$ and $B$ have positive degree $d_A$ and $d_B$, so we have $G=\alpha A^*\beta B^*$ where $A^*$ and $B^*$ have bi-degrees $(a,d_A)$ and $(b,d_B)$, and $\alpha$ and $\beta$ have bi-degrees $(t_\alpha,0)$ and $(t_\beta,0)$. Since $R$ is a UFD, the denominators in the right hand side of the expression $G=\alpha A^*\beta B^*$ must cancel with factors of the numerators of the expression $\alpha A^*\beta B^*$ and this does not affect the values of $d_A$ or $d_B$, so we may assume that $\alpha,\beta, A^*, B^*$ all are in $R$ and $A^*$ and $B^*$ have bi-degrees $(a',d_A)$ and $(b',d_B)$, where the simplification might have changed $a$ and $b$ but will have left $d_a$ and $d_B$ unchanged. Since $d_A$ and $d_B$ are both positive, $G$ has nonunit factors so $G$ is not irreducible. Now note that irreducibility of $G^\circ$ implies that for $(G^\circ)^*$ by (b). Finally, by construction, if $G$ is irreducible with bi-degree $(t,d)$ where $d>0$, then $G=c(G^\circ)^*$ for some nonzero $c\in\KK$, hence $(G)=((G^\circ)^*)$. (d) Since $F\in I_{mP}$, by (a) we have $\frac{F^*}{a_0^s}=(F^*)^\circ\in I_{mP}$, where $(s,d)$ is the bi-degree of $F^*$, and since $d$ is the degree of $(F^*)^\circ$ and since $(F^*)^\circ\in I_{mP}$ we have $d\geq m$. Now let $$D\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)= F^*\big(\frac{a_0}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_0}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)=\frac{F^*(a_0,\ldots,a_n,x_0,\ldots,x_n)}{a_0^sx_0^d},$$ so as a rational function $D$ has bi-degree $(0,0)$, but as a polynomial in $\KK(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})[\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}]$, $D$ has degree $\delta\leq d$. Moreover, since $x_0\not\in I_P$, we have $D\in I_{mQ}$ where $Q$ is the point $Q=(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})$ in the affine open subset $\KK(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})^n$ away from $x_0=0$. Now translate $Q$ to the origin; i.e., consider $$H\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)= D\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}+\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}+\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big).$$ Note that $$a_0^{s+d}x_0^dH=a_0^{s+d}x_0^dF^*\big(\frac{a_0}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_0}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}+\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}+\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)=$$ $$F^*\big(a_0,\ldots,a_n,a_0x_0,a_0x_1+a_1x_0,\ldots,a_0x_n+a_nx_0\big)\in R$$ is a bi-homogeneous polynomial of bi-degree $(s+d,d)$. Since $H$ has multiplicity $m$ at the origin (with respect to the variables $\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}$), $H$ is a sum of terms where each term consists of a monomial in $\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}$ of degree at least $m$ and at most $d$, times a polynomial in the variables $\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}$ of degree at most $s+d$. Thus each term is of the form $$c\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)\big(\frac{x_1}{x_0}\big)^{i_1}\cdots\big(\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)^{i_n}$$ where $m\leq \sum_ji_j\leq d$ and $c$ has degree at most $s+d$. Thus multiplying by $a_0^{s+d}x_0^d$ clears the denominators. Translating back we recover $D$; i.e., $$D\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)= H\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}-\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big),$$ but each term becomes $$c\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)\big(\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\frac{a_1}{a_0}\big)^{i_1}\cdots\big(\frac{x_n}{x_0}-\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)^{i_n} =c\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)\big(\frac{a_0x_1-a_1x_0}{a_0x_0}\big)^{i_1}\cdots\big(\frac{a_0x_n-a_nx_0}{a_0x_0}\big)^{i_n}$$ and multiplying by $a_0^{2d+s}x_0^d$ we obtain $$C(a_0,\ldots,a_n)(a_0x_1-a_1x_0)^{i_1}\cdots(a_0x_n-a_nx_0)^{i_n}$$ where $C$ is homogeneous in the variables $a_i$ of degree $s+d$, and $$(a_0x_1-a_1x_0)^{i_1}\cdots(a_0x_n-a_nx_0)^{i_n}\in J_{mP}.$$ Thus $a_0^{2d+s}x_0^dH\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}-\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)= a_0^{2d+s}x_0^dD=a_0^{2d}F^*\in J_{mP}$. But by \cite[Corollary 7.10]{BV}, since $J_P$ is the ideal generated by the maximal minors of a $2 \times (n+1)$ matrix of indeterminates, namely the two sets of variables, the powers $J_{mP}$ are primary for $J_P$. Since no power of $a_0$ is in $J_{mP}$, we see that $F^*\in J_{mP}$. (e) If $G\in J_{mP}$, then $G=\sum_s H_sM_s$ where each $M_s$ is a product of $m$ forms such as $a_ix_j-a_jx_i$ and each $H_s$ is a bi-homogeneous form of bi-degree $(t-m,d-m)$. So $G^\circ$ is obtained by dividing $G$ by $a_0^t$, hence we get $G^\circ=\sum_s H_s^\circ M_s^\circ$, and each $M_s^\circ$ is a product of $m$ forms such as $(a_ix_j-a_jx_i)/a_0$, each of which is in $I_P$. Thus $G^\circ\in I_{mP}$.
nodes.statement_short: Part-by-part verification: unit factors give (a) and (b), a UFD factorization argument gives (c), and a Taylor translation plus primariness of $J_{mP}$ gives (d) and (e).

But by \cite[Corollary 7.10]{BV}, since $J_P$ is the ideal generated by the maximal minors of a $2 \times (n+1)$ matrix of indeterminates, namely the two sets of variables, the powers $J_{mP}$ are primary for $J_P$. nodes.statement: (e) If $G\in J_{mP}$, then $G=\sum_s H_sM_s$ where each $M_s$ is a product of $m$ forms such as $a_ix_j-a_jx_i$ and each $H_s$ is a bi-homogeneous form of bi-degree $(t-m,d-m)$. nodes.statement: It is shown in \cite{CHMN} that $C=C'\cup \Lambda_1\cup\cdots\cup \Lambda_r$ where $C'$ is unexpected for a subset $Z'$ of $Z$ and has degree $m+1-r$ with a general point $P$ of multiplicity $m-r$ where $r=|Z|-|Z'|$ and each $\Lambda_i$ is the line from $P$ to $p_i$ where $p_1,\ldots, p_r$ are the points of $Z$ not in $Z'$. nodes.name: Proof of the BMSS duality theorem
nodes.statement:
(a) Since $C$ is irreducible, then \cite{CHMN} shows that $C$ is unique. (b) By Lemma ef{StEx}(d) we know that $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m',m+1)$ for some $m'\geq m$ and that $F^*$ has multiplicity at least $m$ in the $a$ variables at $a=x$. The conclusion follows from examining a parameterization given in \cite{CHMN} to conclude that $m'\leq m$. Let $\Lambda$ be the product of the forms defining the lines dual to the points of $Z$. It is not hard to check that there are no unexpected curves for $Z$ with $|Z|<3$, so after a change of coordinates if need be, we may assume $x_0x_1$ divides $\Lambda$. Let $(s_0,s_1,s_2)$ be a syzygy of minimal degree (hence homogeneous of degree $m$; see \cite{CHMN}) for the ideal $(\Lambda_{x_0},\Lambda_{x_1},\Lambda_{x_2})$, where $\Lambda_{x_i}$ denotes the partial with respect to $x_i$; thus $$s_0\Lambda_{x_0}+s_1\Lambda_{x_1}+s_2\Lambda_{x_2}=0.$$ Define $\phi$ formally to be the vector whose components are given by the cross product $$\phi=(\phi_0,\phi_1,\phi_2)=(s_0,s_1,s_2)	imes (x_0,x_1,x_2).$$ Now let $\ell$ be the general line $a_0x_0+a_1x_1+a_2x_2=0$. If $a_2
eq0$, we can parameterize $\ell$ by $(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$, where $(t,s)$ are projective coordinates on $\PP^1$, and by \cite{CHMN} $\phi$ defines a birational map from $\ell$ to $C$. Note that, since $x_0x_1$ divides $\Lambda$, then $x_0$ divides $\Lambda_{x_1}$ and $\Lambda_{x_2}$ and $x_1$ divides $\Lambda_{x_0}$ and $\Lambda_{x_2}$, but $x_0$ does not divide $\Lambda_{x_0}$ and $x_1$ does not divide $\Lambda_{x_1}$. Setting $x_0=0$ in $s_0\Lambda_{x_0}+s_1\Lambda_{x_1}+s_2\Lambda_{x_2}=0$ gives $$s_0\Lambda_{x_0}=0$$ so $x_0$ must divide $s_0$. Similarly, $x_1$ divides $s_1$. Plugging $(x_0,x_1,x_2)=(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$ into $\phi(x_0,x_1,x_2)$ we see from the definition of the cross product that $a_2$ divides $\phi_2(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$, and since $x_i|s_i$ for $i=0,1$, we get that $x_i$ divides $\phi_i$ for $0,1$ and thus after the substitution $(x_0,x_1,x_2)=(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$ that $a_2$ divides $\phi_i$ for $i=0,1,2$. Let $\psi_i=\phi_i/a_2$. Then $\psi_i$ is bi-homogeneous of degree $m-1$ in the $a$ variables and degree $m$ in the variables $s$ and $t$. We also get a parameterization of $C$ using the slope of lines through the point $P=a$. This induces an isomorphism from $E_P$ to $C$, where $E_P$ is the blow up of $P$. But $\psi=(\psi_0,\psi_1,\psi_2)$ induces a birational map $\ell$ to $C$. Composing gives an isomorphism $\ell$ to $E_P$, which is therefore linear. Thus after a change of coordinates fixing $P$ and $x_2=0$, we may assume that the parameterization of $C$ given by $\psi$ is the same as that given by slopes of lines through $P$. In particular, consider the line through the point $(a_1/a_2,a_1/a_2,1)$ with slope $t/s$; in affine coordinates it is $$ rac{x_1}{x_2}- rac{a_1}{a_2}= rac{t}{s}\Big( rac{x_0}{x_2}- rac{a_0}{a_2}\Big)$$ which we can rewrite as $(x_1a_2-a_1x_2)s=t(x_0a_2-a_0x_2)$. Setting $x_2=0$ gives the coordinates $a_2t=x_1, sa_2=x_0$ as the parameterization on $E_P$, and we can assume that the parameterization of $C$ given by mapping the point $(t,s)$ on $E_P$ to the point $(x_0:x_1:x_2)$ where the line $(x_1a_2-a_1x_2)s=t(x_0a_2-a_0x_2)$ meets $C$ (away from $P$) is the same point of $C$ as that given by $\psi(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$. Thus the parameterization is such that $$[x_0:x_1:x_2]=[\psi_0(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t):\psi_1(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t):\psi_2(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)],$$ and hence plugging $s=x_0a_2-a_0x_2$ and $t=x_1a_2-a_1x_2$ in to $(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$ gives $(a_2(x_1a_2-a_1x_2),-a_2(x_0a_2-a_0x_2),a_1x_0a_2-a_0x_1a_2)$, and factoring out the $a_2$ we get $(x_1a_2-a_1x_2,-(x_0a_2-a_0x_2),a_1x_0-a_0x_1)$, each component of which has bi-degree $(1,1)$. So we now have parametric equations for $C$, $$[x_0:x_1:x_2]=[\psi_0(v):\psi_1(v):\psi_2(v)],$$ where $v=(x_1a_2-a_1x_2,-x_0a_2+a_0x_2,a_1x_0-a_0x_1)$, so each component of the right hand side has bi-degree $(m,m+1)$. We get the following equations for $C$ (bi-homogeneous of degree $(m,m+2)$): $x_0\psi_1-x_1\psi_0=0$, $x_0\psi_2-x_2\psi_0=0$, $x_1\psi_2-x_2\psi_1=0$. The form $F^*(a,x)$ defining $C$ is a common divisor of these three equations. Thus $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m',m+1)$ for some $m'\leq m$. Thus $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m,m+1)$, and since it has a point of multiplicity at least $m$ at $a=x$ but degree exactly $m$, the multiplicity is also $m$. (c) Since $F$ has degree $m$ in the $a$ variables, $F$ defines a curve of degree $m$ with a point of multiplicity $m$ at $a=x$, hence it defines a union of $m$ lines through the point $a=x$. The question remains as to what these lines are. To answer this question, translate the point $a=x$ to the point $[1:0:0]$. Doing this gives us $$G(a)=a_0^mF ig(1, rac{a_1}{a_0}+ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{a_2}{a_0}+ rac{x_2}{x_0},1, rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_2}{x_0} ig) \in\KK\Big[ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_2}{x_0}\Big][a_0,a_1,a_2].$$ In the $a$ variables, this defines $m$ lines meeting at $[1:0:0]$. Thus in the $a$ variables $G(a)$ is a homogeneous form of degree $m$, but now the variable $a_0$, which we can regard as defining the line at infinity, does not appear. Note that neither $a_1$ nor $a_2$ is a factor of $G(a)$, since if, say $a_1$ were a factor of $G$, then for all choices of $x$, $G=0$ includes the line from $[1:0:0]$ to $[0:0:1]$. Since the point $[0:0:1]$ is at infinity, it is fixed under the translation we employed, so $F(a_0,a_1,a_2,x_0,x_1,x_2)=0$ includes the line from $[x_0:x_1:x_2]$ to $[0:0:1]$, hence $x_1a_0-x_0a_1$ is a factor of $F$, contradicting the assumption that $C$ is irreducible. Since $a_0$ does not appear in $G(a)$ and $a_1$ and $a_2$ are not factors, we have $G(a)=b_0a_1^m+\cdots+b_ma_2^m$ with $b_i\in\KK ig[ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0} ig]$ and $b_0,b_m
eq0$. Setting $a_2=1$ in $G$ gives $g(a_1)=b_0a_1^m+\cdots+b_m$ and dividing by $b_0$ gives $h(a_1)=g(a_1)/b_0\in\KK( rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0})[a_1]$. Over an appropriate field extension of $\KK( rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0})$ this factors as $h(a_1)=(a_1-h_1)\cdots(a_1-h_m)$. Note that the elements $h_i$ are distinct. If not, then $h$ and hence $g$ has a multiple root, say $h_i$, hence $a_1-h_i$ is a common factor of $g$ and $g'$ (or, taking more derivatives, of $g^{(\mu-1)}$ and $g^{(\mu)}$ if the root has multiplicity $\mu>1$) and thus can be found using the Euclidean algorithm. Thus the linear factor $a_1-h_i$ is in $\KK( rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0})[a_1]$ and so divides $g$ over $\KK( rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0})[a_1]$ and hence $a_1-h_ia_2$ divides $G(a)$ in $\KK ig[ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0} ig][a_0,a_1,a_2]$ and thus $F(a,x)$ as before has a corresponding factor linear in $a$, contrary to assumption. Thus the roots $h_i$ are distinct. Since by Lemma ef{diffMap} the mapping $f$ expressing the coefficients of $h$ as symmetric functions of the roots $h_i$ has an invertible differential $df$ (the roots being distinct), we can by the inverse function theorem \cite[p.\ 33]{FG} regard the roots $h_i$ as holomorphic functions of the coefficients $b_i/b_0$ of $h$. Since each $b_i/b_0$ is a rational (and so holomorphic) function of $x_1/x_0$ and $x_2/x_0$, we can regard the $h_i$ as holomorphic functions of $x_1/x_0$ and $x_2/x_0$. The roots $h_i$ give the points at infinity where $G(a,x)$ vanishes. Specifically these are $[0:h_i:1]$. These are unaffected by affine translations, so the points where $F(a,x)$ vanishes on $a_0=0$ are these same points $[0:h_i:1]$. Thus translating back we see $F(a,x)$ vanishes on the lines through $[x_0:x_1:x_2]$ and $[0:h_i:1]$, so the forms defining these lines divide $F(a,x)$. Specifically, we have $G(a)=b_0(a_1-h_1a_2)\cdots(a_1-h_ma_2)$ so $$b_0\Big( rac{a_1}{a_0}-h_1 rac{a_2}{a_0}\Big)\cdots\Big( rac{a_1}{a_0}-h_m rac{a_2}{a_0}\Big)=G(a)/a_0^m= F\Big(1, rac{a_1}{a_0}+ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{a_2}{a_0}+ rac{x_2}{x_0},1, rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_2}{x_0}\Big)$$ translates back to $$F(a,x)=x_0^{m+1}a_0^mb_0\Big( rac{a_1}{a_0}- rac{x_1}{x_0}- ig( rac{a_2}{a_0}- rac{x_2}{x_0} ig)h_1\Big)\cdots \Big( rac{a_1}{a_0}- rac{x_1}{x_0}- ig( rac{a_2}{a_0}- rac{x_2}{x_0} ig)h_m\Big)=$$ $$x_0b_0 ig((a_1x_0-a_0x_1)-(a_2x_0-a_0x_2)h_1 ig)\cdots  ig((a_1x_0-a_0x_1)-(a_2x_0-a_0x_2)h_m ig)=$$ $$b_0x_0\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_1(x) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|\cdots \left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_m(x) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|.$$ Consider a point $x=a$ where $b_0x_0
eq0$. Then the branches of $F(a,x)=0$ in a neighborhood of $x=a$ are defined by the vanishing of each factor $\lambda_i(x_0,x_1,x_2)=\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_i(x) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|$. The tangent line to the branch $\lambda_i(x)=0$ at $x=a$ is defined by $((
abla \lambda_i)|_{x=a})\cdot (x_0,x_1,x_2)$. Since $\lambda_i=(a_1-a_2h_i)x_0-a_0x_1+a_0x_2h_i$, the gradient $
abla \lambda_i$ is $$\Big((a_1-a_2h_i),-a_0,a_0h_i\Big)+\Big(-a_2h_{i0}x_0+a_0x_2h_{i0},-a_2h_{i1}x_0+a_0x_2h_{i1},-a_2h_{i2}x_0+a_0x_2h_{i2}\Big).$$ The second term vanishes at $x=a$ so $$(
abla \lambda_i)|_{x=a}\cdot(x_0,x_1,x_2)=(a_1-a_2h_i(x),-a_0,a_0h_i(x))|_{x=a}\cdot(x_0,x_1,x_2)=\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_i(a) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|.$$ So we see that the tangent cone to $F(a,x)=0$ at a point $P=a$ such that $b_0x_0
eq0$ is defined by the vanishing of $$F_P(a,x)=b_0(a)a_0\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_1(a) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|\cdots \left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_m(a) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|=$$ $$(-1)^mb_0(a)a_0\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_1(a) & 1\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ \end{array} ight|\cdots \left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_m(a) & 1\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ \end{array} ight|=(-1)^mF(x,a).$$

nodes.statement: (a) Since $C$ is irreducible, then \cite{CHMN} shows that $C$ is unique.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness of an irreducible unexpected curve is CHMN's result.

nodes.name: part (b): lower bound on the bi-degree
nodes.statement: (b) By Lemma \ref{StEx}(d) we know that $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m',m+1)$ for some $m'\geq m$ and that $F^*$ has multiplicity at least $m$ in the $a$ variables at $a=x$. nodes.statement: Let $\Lambda$ be the product of the forms defining the lines dual to the points of $Z$. It is not hard to check that there are no unexpected curves for $Z$ with $|Z|<3$, so after a change of coordinates if need be, we may assume $x_0x_1$ divides $\Lambda$. nodes.statement_short: Take a minimal syzygy of the Jacobian ideal of $\Lambda$ and form $\phi=s\times x$.

nodes.name: parameterize a general line
nodes.statement: Now let $\ell$ be the general line $a_0x_0+a_1x_1+a_2x_2=0$. If $a_2\neq0$, we can parameterize $\ell$ by $(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$, where $(t,s)$ are projective coordinates on $\PP^1$, and by \cite{CHMN} $\phi$ defines a birational map from $\ell$ to $C$.
nodes.statement_short: Parameterize $\ell$ by $(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$; $\phi$ maps it birationally onto $C$.

nodes.name: divisibility of the syzygy components
nodes.statement: Note that, since $x_0x_1$ divides $\Lambda$, then $x_0$ divides $\Lambda_{x_1}$ and $\Lambda_{x_2}$ and $x_1$ divides $\Lambda_{x_0}$ and $\Lambda_{x_2}$, but $x_0$ does not divide $\Lambda_{x_0}$ and $x_1$ does not divide $\Lambda_{x_1}$. Setting $x_0=0$ in $s_0\Lambda_{x_0}+s_1\Lambda_{x_1}+s_2\Lambda_{x_2}=0$ gives $$s_0\Lambda_{x_0}=0$$ so $x_0$ must divide $s_0$. Similarly, $x_1$ divides $s_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Since $x_0x_1\mid\Lambda$, one gets $x_0\mid s_0$ and $x_1\mid s_1$.

nodes.name: divide out $a_2$ to define $\psi$
nodes.statement: Plugging $(x_0,x_1,x_2)=(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$ into $\phi(x_0,x_1,x_2)$ we see from the definition of the cross product that $a_2$ divides $\phi_2(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$, and since $x_i|s_i$ for $i=0,1$, we get that $x_i$ divides $\phi_i$ for $0,1$ and thus after the substitution $(x_0,x_1,x_2)=(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$ that $a_2$ divides $\phi_i$ for $i=0,1,2$. Let $\psi_i=\phi_i/a_2$. Then $\psi_i$ is bi-homogeneous of degree $m-1$ in the $a$ variables and degree $m$ in the variables $s$ and $t$.
nodes.statement_short: $a_2$ divides each $\phi_i$ after substitution, giving $\psi_i$ of bi-degree $(m-1,m)$.

nodes.name: match the two parameterizations
nodes.statement: We also get a parameterization of $C$ using the slope of lines through the point $P=a$. This induces an isomorphism from $E_P$ to $C$, where $E_P$ is the blow up of $P$. But $\psi=(\psi_0,\psi_1,\psi_2)$ induces a birational map $\ell$ to $C$. Composing gives an isomorphism $\ell$ to $E_P$, which is therefore linear. Thus after a change of coordinates fixing $P$ and $x_2=0$, we may assume that the parameterization of $C$ given by $\psi$ is the same as that given by slopes of lines through $P$. In particular, consider the line through the point $(a_1/a_2,a_1/a_2,1)$ with slope $t/s$; in affine coordinates it is $$\frac{x_1}{x_2}-\frac{a_1}{a_2}=\frac{t}{s}\Big(\frac{x_0}{x_2}-\frac{a_0}{a_2}\Big)$$ which we can rewrite as $(x_1a_2-a_1x_2)s=t(x_0a_2-a_0x_2)$. Setting $x_2=0$ gives the coordinates $a_2t=x_1, sa_2=x_0$ as the parameterization on $E_P$, and we can assume that the parameterization of $C$ given by mapping the point $(t,s)$ on $E_P$ to the point $(x_0:x_1:x_2)$ where the line $(x_1a_2-a_1x_2)s=t(x_0a_2-a_0x_2)$ meets $C$ (away from $P$) is the same point of $C$ as that given by $\psi(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$.
nodes.statement_short: The slope parameterization and $\psi$ differ by a linear change of coordinates.

nodes.name: conclude the bi-degree
nodes.statement: Thus the parameterization is such that $$[x_0:x_1:x_2]=[\psi_0(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t):\psi_1(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t):\psi_2(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)],$$ and hence plugging $s=x_0a_2-a_0x_2$ and $t=x_1a_2-a_1x_2$ in to $(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$ gives $(a_2(x_1a_2-a_1x_2),-a_2(x_0a_2-a_0x_2),a_1x_0a_2-a_0x_1a_2)$, and factoring out the $a_2$ we get $(x_1a_2-a_1x_2,-(x_0a_2-a_0x_2),a_1x_0-a_0x_1)$, each component of which has bi-degree $(1,1)$. So we now have parametric equations for $C$, $$[x_0:x_1:x_2]=[\psi_0(v):\psi_1(v):\psi_2(v)],$$ where $v=(x_1a_2-a_1x_2,-x_0a_2+a_0x_2,a_1x_0-a_0x_1)$, so each component of the right hand side has bi-degree $(m,m+1)$. We get the following equations for $C$ (bi-homogeneous of degree $(m,m+2)$): $x_0\psi_1-x_1\psi_0=0$, $x_0\psi_2-x_2\psi_0=0$, $x_1\psi_2-x_2\psi_1=0$. The form $F^*(a,x)$ defining $C$ is a common divisor of these three equations. Thus $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m',m+1)$ for some $m'\leq m$. Thus $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m,m+1)$, and since it has a point of multiplicity at least $m$ at $a=x$ but degree exactly $m$, the multiplicity is also $m$.
nodes.statement_short: Substituting $v$ gives equations of bi-degree $(m,m+2)$, forcing $F^*$ to have bi-degree $(m,m+1)$ with an $m$-fold point at $a=x$.

nodes.name: part (c): $F$ is a union of $m$ lines in $a$
nodes.statement: (c) Since $F$ has degree $m$ in the $a$ variables, $F$ defines a curve of degree $m$ with a point of multiplicity $m$ at $a=x$, hence it defines a union of $m$ lines through the point $a=x$.
nodes.statement_short: Degree $m$ with an $m$-fold point means $m$ concurrent lines.

nodes.name: translate $a=x$ to $[1:0:0]$
nodes.statement: The question remains as to what these lines are. To answer this question, translate the point $a=x$ to the point $[1:0:0]$. Doing this gives us $$G(a)=a_0^mF\big(1,\frac{a_1}{a_0}+\frac{x_1}{x_0},\frac{a_2}{a_0}+\frac{x_2}{x_0},1,\frac{x_1}{x_0},\frac{x_2}{x_0}\big) \in\KK\Big[\frac{x_1}{x_0},\frac{x_2}{x_0}\Big][a_0,a_1,a_2].$$ In the $a$ variables, this defines $m$ lines meeting at $[1:0:0]$. Thus in the $a$ variables $G(a)$ is a homogeneous form of degree $m$, but now the variable $a_0$, which we can regard as defining the line at infinity, does not appear. Note that neither $a_1$ nor $a_2$ is a factor of $G(a)$, since if, say $a_1$ were a factor of $G$, then for all choices of $x$, $G=0$ includes the line from $[1:0:0]$ to $[0:0:1]$. Since the point $[0:0:1]$ is at infinity, it is fixed under the translation we employed, so $F(a_0,a_1,a_2,x_0,x_1,x_2)=0$ includes the line from $[x_0:x_1:x_2]$ to $[0:0:1]$, hence $x_1a_0-x_0a_1$ is a factor of $F$, contradicting the assumption that $C$ is irreducible.
nodes.statement_short: After translation, $a_0$ disappears from $G(a)$ and neither $a_1$ nor $a_2$ can be a factor.

nodes.name: the roots $h_i$ are distinct
nodes.statement: Since $a_0$ does not appear in $G(a)$ and $a_1$ and $a_2$ are not factors, we have $G(a)=b_0a_1^m+\cdots+b_ma_2^m$ with $b_i\in\KK\big[\frac{x_1}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}\big]$ and $b_0,b_m\neq0$. Setting $a_2=1$ in $G$ gives $g(a_1)=b_0a_1^m+\cdots+b_m$ and dividing by $b_0$ gives $h(a_1)=g(a_1)/b_0\in\KK(\frac{x_1}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0})[a_1]$. Over an appropriate field extension of $\KK(\frac{x_1}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0})$ this factors as $h(a_1)=(a_1-h_1)\cdots(a_1-h_m)$. Note that the elements $h_i$ are distinct. If not, then $h$ and hence $g$ has a multiple root, say $h_i$, hence $a_1-h_i$ is a common factor of $g$ and $g'$ (or, taking more derivatives, of $g^{(\mu-1)}$ and $g^{(\mu)}$ if the root has multiplicity $\mu>1$) and thus can be found using the Euclidean algorithm. Thus the linear factor $a_1-h_i$ is in $\KK(\frac{x_1}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0})[a_1]$ and so divides $g$ over $\KK(\frac{x_1}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0})[a_1]$ and hence $a_1-h_ia_2$ divides $G(a)$ in $\KK\big[\frac{x_1}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}\big][a_0,a_1,a_2]$ and thus $F(a,x)$ as before has a corresponding factor linear in $a$, contrary to assumption. Thus the roots $h_i$ are distinct.
nodes.statement_short: A repeated root would produce a linear factor of $F$ in $a$, contradicting irreducibility.

nodes.name: the roots depend holomorphically on $x$
nodes.statement: Since by Lemma \ref{diffMap} the mapping $f$ expressing the coefficients of $h$ as symmetric functions of the roots $h_i$ has an invertible differential $df$ (the roots being distinct), we can by the inverse function theorem \cite[p.\ 33]{FG} regard the roots $h_i$ as holomorphic functions of the coefficients $b_i/b_0$ of $h$. Since each $b_i/b_0$ is a rational (and so holomorphic) function of $x_1/x_0$ and $x_2/x_0$, we can regard the $h_i$ as holomorphic functions of $x_1/x_0$ and $x_2/x_0$.
nodes.statement_short: The Vandermonde lemma plus the inverse function theorem make the $h_i$ holomorphic in $x_1/x_0,x_2/x_0$.

nodes.name: identify the lines of $F$
nodes.statement: The roots $h_i$ give the points at infinity where $G(a,x)$ vanishes. Specifically these are $[0:h_i:1]$. These are unaffected by affine translations, so the points where $F(a,x)$ vanishes on $a_0=0$ are these same points $[0:h_i:1]$. Thus translating back we see $F(a,x)$ vanishes on the lines through $[x_0:x_1:x_2]$ and $[0:h_i:1]$, so the forms defining these lines divide $F(a,x)$.
nodes.statement_short: $F(a,x)$ vanishes on the lines joining $[x_0:x_1:x_2]$ to the points $[0:h_i:1]$.

nodes.name: determinant factorization of $F$
nodes.statement: Specifically, we have $G(a)=b_0(a_1-h_1a_2)\cdots(a_1-h_ma_2)$ so $$b_0\Big(\frac{a_1}{a_0}-h_1\frac{a_2}{a_0}\Big)\cdots\Big(\frac{a_1}{a_0}-h_m\frac{a_2}{a_0}\Big)=G(a)/a_0^m= F\Big(1,\frac{a_1}{a_0}+\frac{x_1}{x_0},\frac{a_2}{a_0}+\frac{x_2}{x_0},1,\frac{x_1}{x_0},\frac{x_2}{x_0}\Big)$$ translates back to $$F(a,x)=x_0^{m+1}a_0^mb_0\Big(\frac{a_1}{a_0}-\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\big(\frac{a_2}{a_0}-\frac{x_2}{x_0}\big)h_1\Big)\cdots \Big(\frac{a_1}{a_0}-\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\big(\frac{a_2}{a_0}-\frac{x_2}{x_0}\big)h_m\Big)=$$ $$x_0b_0\big((a_1x_0-a_0x_1)-(a_2x_0-a_0x_2)h_1\big)\cdots \big((a_1x_0-a_0x_1)-(a_2x_0-a_0x_2)h_m\big)=$$ $$b_0x_0\left|\begin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_1(x) & 1\\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\\ \end{array} \right|\cdots \left|\begin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_m(x) & 1\\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\\ \end{array} \right|.$$
nodes.statement_short: Write $F(a,x)$ as $b_0x_0$ times a product of $3\times3$ determinants.

nodes.name: tangent lines to the branches
nodes.statement:
Consider a point $x=a$ where $b_0x_0
eq0$. Then the branches of $F(a,x)=0$ in a neighborhood of $x=a$ are defined by the vanishing of each factor $\lambda_i(x_0,x_1,x_2)=\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_i(x) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|$. The tangent line to the branch $\lambda_i(x)=0$ at $x=a$ is defined by $((
abla \lambda_i)|_{x=a})\cdot (x_0,x_1,x_2)$. Since $\lambda_i=(a_1-a_2h_i)x_0-a_0x_1+a_0x_2h_i$, the gradient $
abla \lambda_i$ is $$\Big((a_1-a_2h_i),-a_0,a_0h_i\Big)+\Big(-a_2h_{i0}x_0+a_0x_2h_{i0},-a_2h_{i1}x_0+a_0x_2h_{i1},-a_2h_{i2}x_0+a_0x_2h_{i2}\Big).$$ The second term vanishes at $x=a$ so $$(
abla \lambda_i)|_{x=a}\cdot(x_0,x_1,x_2)=(a_1-a_2h_i(x),-a_0,a_0h_i(x))|_{x=a}\cdot(x_0,x_1,x_2)=\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_i(a) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|.$$
nodes.statement_short: Each branch $\lambda_i=0$ has tangent line given by the gradient at $x=a$.

nodes.name: conclude the tangent cone equals $(-1)^mF(x,a)$
nodes.statement: So we see that the tangent cone to $F(a,x)=0$ at a point $P=a$ such that $b_0x_0\neq0$ is defined by the vanishing of $$F_P(a,x)=b_0(a)a_0\left|\begin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_1(a) & 1\\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\\ \end{array} \right|\cdots \left|\begin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_m(a) & 1\\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\\ \end{array} \right|=$$ $$(-1)^mb_0(a)a_0\left|\begin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_1(a) & 1\\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\\ \end{array} \right|\cdots \left|\begin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_m(a) & 1\\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\\ \end{array} \right|=(-1)^mF(x,a).$$
nodes.statement_short: Swapping the last two rows of each determinant yields the sign $(-1)^m$ and the form $F(x,a)$.

nodes.name: universal script for detecting unexpected hypersurfaces
nodes.statement: for n from 2 to 6 do { -- Loop over dim 2 to 6 R=QQ[x_0..x_n]; -- Define coordinate ring S=frac(QQ[a_0..a_n]); --Define ring for generic point CODE BLOCK for Pts={...}; -- Insert the list of the points of Z here print {"n=",n,"#Pts=",#Pts}; -- Print completion status indicator for d from 2 to 6 do { -- Loop over degree Md=flatten entries(basis(d,R)); -- Create deg d monomial basis for m from 2 to d do { -- Loop over multiplicity m print {"d=",d,"m=",m}; -- Print completion status indicator Mm=flatten entries(basis(m-1,R)); -- Create deg m-1 monomial basis A={}; -- A will contain the list of rows for transpose of matrix Q1 apply(Md,i->(N={};for s from 0 to #Pts-1 do N=N|{sub(i,matrix{Pts_s})};A=A|{N})); D={}; -- D will contain the list of rows for transpose of matrix Q2 apply(Md,i->(N={};for s from 0 to #Mm-1 do N=N|{diff(Mm_s,i)};D=D|{N})); Q1=transpose matrix A; -- Q1 is defined over R Q2=transpose matrix D; -- Q2 is defined over R M={}; for i from 0 to n do M=M|{a_i}; -- M is the coord vector for generic point Q1S=sub(Q1,S); -- Q1 is now defined to be over S Q2S=sub(Q2,matrix{M}); -- Swap x variables for a variables N=Q1S||Q2S; expdim=#Md - (rank Q1S) - (rank Q2S); actdim=#Md-(rank N); if actdim > expdim and actdim > 0 then print {"n=",n,"d=",d,"m=",m,"edim=",expdim,"adim=",actdim}}}}
nodes.statement_short: Macaulay2 script that builds the condition matrix $N$ for $Z$ and a generic fat point, then reports every $(n,d,m)$ whose actual kernel dimension exceeds the expected one.
input: the list of the points of $Z$
output: the vector space of unexpected forms has expected dimension edim and actual dimension adim

nodes.name: define the coordinate ring
nodes.statement: R=QQ[x_0..x_n]; -- Define coordinate ring
nodes.statement_short: Coordinate ring over $\QQ$.

nodes.name: define the ring for the generic point
nodes.statement: S=frac(QQ[a_0..a_n]); --Define ring for generic point
nodes.statement_short: Fraction field in the $a_i$.

nodes.name: insert the points of $Z$
nodes.statement: CODE BLOCK for Pts={...}; -- Insert the list of the points of Z here
nodes.statement_short: Plug in the list of points of $Z$.

nodes.name: degree $d$ monomial basis
nodes.statement: Md=flatten entries(basis(d,R)); -- Create deg d monomial basis
nodes.statement_short: Build the monomial basis in degree $d$.

nodes.name: degree $m-1$ monomial basis
nodes.statement: Mm=flatten entries(basis(m-1,R)); -- Create deg m-1 monomial basis
nodes.statement_short: Monomial basis in degree $m-1$.

nodes.name: build the point-condition rows
nodes.statement: A={}; -- A will contain the list of rows for transpose of matrix Q1 apply(Md,i->(N={};for s from 0 to #Pts-1 do N=N|{sub(i,matrix{Pts_s})};A=A|{N}));
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate each degree-$d$ monomial at each point of $Z$ to fill $Q_1$.

nodes.name: build the multiplicity-condition rows
nodes.statement: D={}; -- D will contain the list of rows for transpose of matrix Q2 apply(Md,i->(N={};for s from 0 to #Mm-1 do N=N|{diff(Mm_s,i)};D=D|{N}));
nodes.statement_short: Take order $m-1$ partials of each degree-$d$ monomial to fill $Q_2$.

nodes.name: assemble the matrices over $S$
nodes.statement: Q1=transpose matrix A; -- Q1 is defined over R Q2=transpose matrix D; -- Q2 is defined over R M={}; for i from 0 to n do M=M|{a_i}; -- M is the coord vector for generic point Q1S=sub(Q1,S); -- Q1 is now defined to be over S Q2S=sub(Q2,matrix{M}); -- Swap x variables for a variables
nodes.statement_short: Transpose and base-change $Q_1,Q_2$, substituting $a_i$ for $x_i$ in the partials.

nodes.name: compare expected and actual dimensions
nodes.statement: N=Q1S||Q2S; expdim=#Md - (rank Q1S) - (rank Q2S); actdim=#Md-(rank N);
nodes.statement_short: Compute expected and actual dimensions.

nodes.name: report unexpected cases
nodes.statement: if actdim > expdim and actdim > 0 then print {"n=",n,"d=",d,"m=",m,"edim=",expdim,"adim=",actdim}}}}
nodes.statement_short: Print $(n,d,m,edim,adim)$ whenever the actual dimension exceeds the expected one.

nodes.name: CODE BLOCK generating $Z_{B_{n+1}}$
nodes.statement: H={}; W1=subsets(n+1,1); apply(W1,s->(H=H|{x_(s_0)})); W2=subsets(n+1,2); apply(W2,s->(H=H|{x_(s_0)+x_(s_1),x_(s_0)-x_(s_1)})); Pts={}; for j from 0 to #H-1 do (v={};for i from 0 to n do (v=v|{diff(x_i,H_j)});Pts=Pts|{v});
nodes.statement_short: Generates the points dual to the $B_{n+1}$ hyperplane arrangement as the gradients of the forms $x_i$, $x_i\pm x_j$.

nodes.name: the coordinate hyperplanes
nodes.statement: H={}; W1=subsets(n+1,1); apply(W1,s->(H=H|{x_(s_0)}));
nodes.statement_short: Collect the linear forms $x_i$.

nodes.name: the forms $x_i\pm x_j$
nodes.statement_short: Append the forms $x_i+x_j$ and $x_i-x_j$.

nodes.name: dualize to points
nodes.statement: Pts={}; for j from 0 to #H-1 do (v={};for i from 0 to n do (v=v|{diff(x_i,H_j)});Pts=Pts|{v});
nodes.statement_short: Take gradients to get the dual point coordinates.

nodes.name: CODE BLOCK generating $Z_{D_{n+1}}$
nodes.statement: H={}; W2=subsets(n+1,2); apply(W2,s->(H=H|{x_(s_0)+x_(s_1),x_(s_0)-x_(s_1)})); Pts={}; for j from 0 to #H-1 do (v={}; for i from 0 to n do (v=v|{diff(x_i,H_j)});Pts=Pts|{v});
nodes.statement_short: Generates the points dual to the $D_{n+1}$ arrangement using only the forms $x_i\pm x_j$.

nodes.name: set up the pairs
nodes.statement: H={}; W2=subsets(n+1,2);
nodes.statement_short: Enumerate index pairs.

nodes.name: the forms $x_i\pm x_j$
nodes.statement_short: Collect the forms $x_i+x_j$ and $x_i-x_j$.

nodes.name: dualize to points
nodes.statement: Pts={}; for j from 0 to #H-1 do (v={}; for i from 0 to n do (v=v|{diff(x_i,H_j)});Pts=Pts|{v});
nodes.statement_short: Take gradients to get the dual point coordinates.
